prompt.context: Our client is Down Under Apparel, an Australian-based swimwear and lifestyle company. The company unexpectedly missed its internal earnings target. The CEO has called on your firm to diagnose the problem.
prompt.question: Why did Down Under miss its earnings forecast, and what should the client do to position itself more successfully in the short and long term?

clarifying_info.q: Who are Down Under's main competitors?
clarifying_info.a: Maui is the largest rival in the surf and athletic swimwear category but offers lower quality products at lower price points. The client has no interest in growth through competitor acquisition.

Surfers and Professional Athletes (30% of revenue) — willing to pay for performance, though average surfer income limits spend. Luxury Seekers (70% of revenue) — fastest-growing segment, casual users who value the brand and aesthetics.

clarifying_info.q: What sales channels does Down Under use?
clarifying_info.a: Surf Shops (small independent retailers in beach towns, carry limited merchandise, almost exclusively performance wear); Big Box Retailers (price-sensitive customers, wide variety including equipment, frequent sales); Department Stores (least price-sensitive, focus on lifestyle wear, only channel outside online offering 'resort collection'); Direct to Consumer / Online (repeat customers, never puts anything on sale).

exhibits.title: Sales and Costs by Year (2012–2014)
exhibits.shows: Two bar charts side by side: (1) Sales by Year with Forecast vs Actual bars for 2012, 2013, and 2014; (2) Costs by Year with Forecast vs Actual bars for 2012, 2013, and 2014.

exhibits.title: Forecast Details (Handout 2)
exhibits.shows: A handout with additional forecast breakdown details for 2014.

exhibits.title: Sales by Category (Actuals), Average Price by Category (2014), and Margin by Category
exhibits.shows: Three charts: (1) Net Sales by Category (bar chart, 2012–2014) broken out into Casual Swim, Professional Swim, Resort Wear, Beach Attire, and Surf Equipment; (2) Average Price by Category for 2014; (3) Margin by Category (bar chart).

exhibits.title: Cost Information (Actuals) by Category
exhibits.shows: A grouped bar chart showing average cost by category broken into Materials, Labor, Marketing, Shipping, and SG&A, plus additional notes on Down Under's cost structure and manufacturing plans.

data.note: Costs broken into Materials, Labor, Marketing, Shipping, SG&A by category. FY2014 costs approximately equal FY2013 costs. Down Under offers free shipping for Direct to Consumer sales. Company is evaluating three sites for a new manufacturing/distribution center: Southern California, Mexico, Guatemala. Five years ago manufacturing relocated from Australia to South Asia.

framework: Diagnose the earnings gap: compare forecast vs actual sales and costs to isolate the source of the miss
Analyze sales by channel and by product category to identify where shortfall occurred
Examine costs by category to determine whether costs are the driver or if it is revenue-side
Identify the new Surf Equipment category launch as a key variable and assess its performance
Evaluate risks and challenges of the new product category and distribution channel
Develop short- and long-term recommendations to improve performance

questions.prompt: Calculate the expected earnings based on Exhibit 1 and identify the size of the earnings gap.
questions.guidance: Candidate should subtract forecast costs from forecast sales to get expected earnings, then subtract actual costs from actual sales to get actual earnings, and compare. Expected earnings = $12,800M - $11,700M = $1,100M. Actual earnings = $12,000M - $11,500M = $500M. Earnings gap = $600M.

math.setup: Expected earnings = Forecast Sales - Forecast Costs; Actual earnings = Actual Sales - Actual Costs; Gap = Expected - Actual
math.answer: Down Under missed its earnings target by $600 million

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 3, what do you notice about the sales by category, and what stands out?
questions.guidance: Candidate should notice that Surf Equipment appears as a new category in 2014 (not present in prior years). This signals a new product launch. Candidate should flag this for investigation and ask the interviewer for more detail about the Surf Equipment category.

questions.prompt: After identifying Surf Equipment as a new category, the interviewer reveals: Surf Equipment is a recently launched category; products include surfboards, primarily sold at Surf Shops; Down Under sold $800M at Surf Shops in 2014. What does this tell you about the shortfall?
questions.guidance: Candidate should compare actual Surf Equipment sales ($800M at Surf Shops) to the total Surf Equipment revenue in Exhibit 3 ($1,200M). Alternatively, probe what the forecast for Surf Equipment was to determine the miss. The key insight is that the new product launch underperformed at the surf shop channel, and this category was expected to drive significant incremental revenue. At $400 average price, the shortfall of ~$800M implies roughly 2 million fewer surfboards/equipment units sold than forecast.

math.setup: Shortfall in Surf Equipment = Forecast Surf Equipment sales - Actual Surf Equipment sales at Surf Shops. If forecast assumed higher volumes, the gap is driven by lower-than-expected unit sales. Using average price: $800M shortfall / $400 avg price = 2M fewer units.
steps: Revenue shortfall attributable to Surf Equipment ≈ $800M (gap between plan and actual at Surf Shops)
math.answer: The client missed its earnings forecast primarily due to selling approximately 2 million fewer surfboards/surf equipment units than expected at Surf Shops

questions.prompt: Looking at Exhibit 4, are costs the issue? What do you observe?
questions.guidance: Candidate should note that FY2014 costs are approximately equal to FY2013 costs. The main cost anomaly is higher marketing costs as a percentage of overall costs, attributable to the recent Surf Equipment product launch. Costs are not the primary driver of the earnings miss.

brainstorming.prompt: What strategies should Down Under pursue to increase sales and successfully grow the Surf Equipment category, and what are the key considerations or challenges?

categories.name: Channel Strategy
ideas: Expand Surf Equipment distribution beyond Surf Shops to Big Box Retailers where broader customer base exists
Leverage online Direct to Consumer channel to sell surf equipment directly, avoiding margin sharing
Negotiate better shelf placement and merchandising support at existing Surf Shop partners
Consider pop-up or experiential retail in high-traffic beach markets

categories.name: Product & Pricing
ideas: Review $400 average price point against customer willingness to pay at each channel
Introduce entry-level surfboard SKU to attract price-sensitive Big Box customers
Bundle surf equipment with swimwear to increase average transaction value
Expand equipment range beyond boards to accessories (leashes, wax, fins)

categories.name: Marketing & Brand
ideas: Invest in athlete endorsements and surf culture partnerships to establish credibility in equipment
Run targeted campaigns at surf events and competitions to reach core surfer segment
Leverage Luxury Seeker segment's brand loyalty to promote aspirational surf equipment
Increase digital marketing spend targeting surf lifestyle communities

categories.name: Customer Segments
ideas: Focus initially on Surfers and Professional Athletes (30% of revenue) as core early adopters for equipment
Develop aspirational messaging for Luxury Seekers who want the lifestyle without professional expertise
Create loyalty program for repeat equipment buyers

categories.name: Operational Considerations
ideas: New manufacturing/distribution center location choice (Southern California, Mexico, Guatemala) will affect shipping cost and lead times for bulky equipment
Free shipping for DTC channel adds cost burden for large/heavy surf equipment items — consider modifying policy for equipment
Ensure quality control for safety-critical surf equipment to protect brand reputation

recommendation: Down Under missed its earnings forecast primarily due to lower-than-expected Surf Equipment sales at Surf Shops, resulting in approximately $600M earnings gap and ~2 million fewer units sold than planned
In the short term, Down Under should broaden Surf Equipment distribution to Big Box Retailers and the DTC online channel to reach more customers beyond the limited Surf Shop footprint

In the long term, Down Under should invest in athlete marketing to build category credibility, optimize its Surf Equipment price architecture, and leverage its Luxury Seeker customer base to drive aspirational equipment sales
risks: Surf Shops are the client's core relationship channel — expanding aggressively to Big Box could strain those partnerships
Surf Equipment is a tangential category to apparel; quality and safety standards for boards are different and brand risk is higher if products underperform
Free DTC shipping economics worsen significantly for bulky, heavy surfboards
Maui competes in this space at lower price points, limiting Down Under's ability to capture price-sensitive customers
Manufacturing center location choice will have long-term cost implications — wrong site selection could erode the profitability advantage of Surf Equipment's 20% margin
next_steps: Conduct channel-by-channel demand analysis to size the opportunity in Big Box and DTC for Surf Equipment
Evaluate manufacturing/distribution site options (Southern California, Mexico, Guatemala) through a cost-benefit lens specific to surf equipment logistics
Pilot a Big Box Retailer test for Surf Equipment in 2–3 markets before full rollout
Review DTC shipping policy for oversized items to protect margins
